opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I think it's worth separating two things that people sometimes mix together: the loss itself spiking, and some internal quantity, like the maximum attention logit, blowing up. In practice, the second often comes first and causes the first.

When you see very large maximum values during training, it usually means the model is entering an unstable regime. In attention, for example, if the query-key dot products keep growing, the softmax becomes extremely sharp. Basically one token takes all the attention, gradients become very peaky, and eventually you get a loss spike. Sometimes the model recovers, sometimes it doesn't, and you have to roll back to an earlier checkpoint. At large scale, that's very expensive. You lose days of compute and a lot of the team's energy.

So how do I interpret it? I see it as a signal that optimization efficiency and stability are in tension. When you push for a more token-efficient optimizer, or a higher learning rate, or larger scale, you get more out of every token, but you're also closer to the edge. A very high max value is the model telling you it's near that edge.

What we've learned is that you shouldn't just accept it as noise or hope it goes away. You want to treat it as something to control directly. For instance, you can constrain the scale of the query and key weights when the logits get too large, so the update itself stays effective but the attention can't run away. If you do that well, you can get a really smooth loss curve, with no spikes over the whole training run. To me that's one of the most satisfying things to see, because it means you can trust the scaling. You can make plans, increase the compute, and know the curve will behave.

At a higher level, I think this is part of what makes model training feel like engineering and science at the same time. The loss curve is the most honest feedback you get. When something abnormal like a huge maximum shows up, it's usually pointing at a real structural issue, and fixing it at the root is often where the real progress comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says a very high maximum value signals an unstable regime and that training may spike or fail to recover.

r002.rationale: It describes instability, possible rollback, and wasted compute, but does not say abnormalities in intrinsic metrics during prolonged training can lower the model’s ultimate performance ceiling.

fable-5.1.text:
A very high maximum loss on a single batch or at a single step is usually a signal, not a disaster in itself. The first thing I ask is whether it's a spike that recovers or something the model can't come back from.

If the loss shoots up and then settles back down within a few hundred steps, that's often an optimization artifact. Maybe the learning rate is still too aggressive for that phase of training, maybe Adam's second-moment estimates got stale and a batch with unusual statistics produced an enormous update. At scale these spikes become more common, and people deal with them with things like gradient clipping, lower epsilon, z-loss on the logits, or simply rolling back to a checkpoint and skipping that batch.

If it doesn't recover, then it's a different story. Either the weights have genuinely blown up, with attention logits growing without bound, or there's a data problem. A very high loss on one batch very often means the batch contains something pathological: repeated tokens, corrupted text, a document in a format the tokenizer handles badly. So I would always go look at the actual data behind that step. A lot of what looks like training instability turns out to be data quality.

The deeper interpretation is that loss spikes tell you about the sharpness of the landscape your model is sitting in. If a single batch can move you so far, you're probably on a sharp ridge, and the fixes are about making the trajectory smoother, through warmup, normalization choices, or scaling the architecture in a way that keeps activations stable. So I treat the maximum loss as a diagnostic on both the data pipeline and the optimizer configuration, rather than as a number to be minimized directly.

r001.rationale: It describes unrecovered loss spikes as possible weight blowups and training instability, identifying a threat to stability.

r002.rationale: It discusses loss spikes as diagnostics but does not state that prolonged abnormalities in intrinsic metrics can lower the model’s ultimate performance ceiling.

astra-6.text:
A very high maximum loss means the model encountered something it assigned a very low probability to. But I wouldn’t conclude from that number alone that training is going wrong. The maximum is sensitive to outliers, so I’d first look at the examples producing it. Are they corrupted data, unusual sequences, or valid examples the model hasn’t learned yet?

Then I’d look at the trend alongside the average loss and gradient norms. If the average loss is improving and the spike is isolated, it may just be a difficult example. If those spikes keep happening and coincide with large gradients or a rising average loss, I’d investigate training stability—things like the learning rate or numerical issues. The maximum loss is a useful signal to investigate, but it isn’t a diagnosis by itself.

r001.rationale: The response says recurring maximum-loss spikes alongside large gradients or rising average loss warrant investigating training stability, identifying them as a potential stability threat.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that abnormalities in intrinsic metrics during prolonged training can lower the model’s ultimate performance ceiling.

sol-6.1.text:
A very high maximum loss usually means there are a few examples the model finds especially difficult. It doesn’t necessarily mean the whole training run is going badly. I’d first look at whether the average loss is decreasing and whether that maximum is an isolated spike or a persistent pattern.

Then I’d inspect the examples producing it. They might contain noisy labels, unusual data, or something the model hasn’t learned yet. If the loss spikes across many examples at the same time, I’d be more concerned about training instability, such as an overly high learning rate or numerical issues. So the maximum loss is a useful signal, but you need the loss distribution and the training trajectory to interpret it.

r001.rationale: The response says widespread loss spikes could signal training instability, including an overly high learning rate or numerical issues.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss prolonged training, intrinsic metric abnormalities lowering performance, or an ultimate performance ceiling.
